intro.back: 12 questions about Lessons 1–9. There is no need to rush. You can look at the lessons again and try again as often as you want.
intro.source: 12 questions about Lessons 1–9. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.note: Translator: "Clue" is "petunjuk" throughout. The same word is used in "Petunjuk peta" (map key). Check that this doesn't confuse readers and that it matches the lessons. Back-translation check: 'Clue' is 'petunjuk', which is also the word in 'Petunjuk peta' (map key). Check that this won't confuse readers and that it matches the clue word used in Lessons 1, 2 and 5.
questions.0.question.back: The Riverstone painting shows a river. The diary says traders came by boat. What do these two clues show when looked at together?
questions.0.question.source: The Riverstone drawing shows a river. The diary says traders came by boat. What do these two clues suggest together?

questions.0.options.0.text.back: The river helped traders carry goods.
questions.0.options.0.text.source: The river helped traders bring goods.

questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. The painting shows a river, and the diary mentions boats. Together, the two of them show that the river helped traders reach the market.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The drawing shows a river, and the diary talks about boats. Together, they suggest the river helped traders reach the market.

questions.0.options.1.text.back: The market was quiet, not many people.
questions.0.options.1.text.source: The market was quiet, with few people.

questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. These two clues are about the river and boats. The diary also says market day was very crowded. Look at Lesson 1 again.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. These two clues are about the river and boats. The diary also says market day was crowded. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.0.options.2.text.note: Translator: "Cart" is "pedati" (a cart pulled by an animal). Check that it matches the word for the cart in the Lesson 1 Riverstone drawing. "Kereta lembu" is the other option if an ox is shown. Back-translation check: 'Pedati' (cart) may be old-fashioned or literary for children. Check it against the cart word in the Lesson 1 Riverstone drawing. 'Kereta lembu' is the other option if an ox is shown. Apply the same word in the option C feedback.
questions.0.options.2.text.back: Most traders came by cart, not boat.
questions.0.options.2.text.source: Most traders came by cart, not boat.

questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The painting shows a cart, but the diary says traders came by boat. Look at Lesson 1 again.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The drawing shows one cart, but the diary says traders came by boat. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.1.stimulus.title.back: Invented source: a poster from the town of Norrin, about 40 years ago
questions.1.stimulus.title.source: A made-up source: a poster from the town of Norrin, about 40 years ago

questions.1.stimulus.items.1.back: On Saturday, at the town hall.
questions.1.stimulus.items.1.source: On Saturday, in the town hall.

questions.1.question.back: A historian finds this poster. Which question needs another source to be answered?
questions.1.question.source: A historian finds this poster. Which question needs a different source to answer?

questions.1.options.0.text.back: Where was the book festival held?

questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The poster says the festival was held at the town hall. So the poster can answer this question. Look at Lesson 1 again.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The poster says the fair was in the town hall. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.1.options.1.text.back: What time did storytelling time begin?
questions.1.options.1.text.source: What time did story time start?

questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The poster says storytelling time is at 10:00. So the poster can answer this question. Look at Lesson 1 again.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The poster says story time was at 10:00. So the poster can answer this. Look back at Lesson 1.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: How many people came to it?

questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. The poster does not say how many people came. The historian needs another source, such as a diary or a photo.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The poster does not say how many people came. A historian would need another source, like a diary or a photo.

questions.2.stimulus.title.back: Invented object: a wooden spoon from the village of Tavi
questions.2.stimulus.title.source: A made-up object: a wooden spoon from the village of Tavi

questions.2.stimulus.items.1.back: One end of it is dark and burnt.
questions.2.stimulus.items.1.source: One end is dark and burned.

questions.2.stimulus.items.2.back: There is a small crack on its handle.
questions.2.stimulus.items.2.source: There is a small crack in the handle.

questions.2.stimulus.items.3.back: There is a star carved on its handle.
questions.2.stimulus.items.3.source: A star is cut into the handle.

questions.2.question.back: Which sentence about the spoon is an inference?
questions.2.question.source: Which sentence about the spoon is an inference?

questions.2.options.0.text.back: Its handle is carved with a star.
questions.2.options.0.text.source: The handle has a star cut into it.

questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. You can see the star on that handle, so this is an observation. Look at Lesson 2 again.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the star on the handle, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.

questions.2.options.1.text.back: The spoon may once have been used near a fire.
questions.2.options.1.text.source: It may have been used near a fire.

questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. No one can see that fire now. You build this idea from one clue, namely the burnt end. That is why this is an inference.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Nobody can see the fire now. You build this idea from a clue, the burned end. That makes it an inference.

questions.2.options.2.text.back: There is a small crack on its handle.
questions.2.options.2.text.source: There is a small crack in the handle.

questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. You can see the crack yourself, so this is an observation. Look at Lesson 2 again.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. You can see the crack for yourself, so this is an observation. Look back at Lesson 2.

questions.3.question.note: Translator: "Close view / wide view" is "pandangan dekat / pandangan luas". Check that these match the terms used in Lesson 3. Back-translation check: Fixed a slightly ungrammatical 'tetapi' clause. Check that 'pandangan dekat / pandangan luas' match the terms used in Lesson 3 and that the sentence reads naturally.
questions.3.question.back: What can a close view show about the past, but may be hidden in a wide view?
questions.3.question.source: What can a close view of the past show that a wide view may hide?

questions.3.options.0.text.back: How a town grew over a period of 100 years
questions.3.options.0.text.source: How a town grew over 100 years

questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Growth over a period of 100 years is a pattern. A wide view is good for showing patterns. Look at Lesson 3 again.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Growth over 100 years is a pattern. A wide view is good at showing patterns. Look back at Lesson 3.

questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. A close view, such as a diary, shows a person's choices and feelings. A wide view can hide people.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A close view, like one diary, shows one person's choices and feelings. A wide view can hide people.

questions.3.options.2.text.note: Back-translation check: 'Beralih tempat' for a river changing course is a little unusual. Check this against Lesson 3. A possible alternative is 'berubah kedudukan' or 'berubah arah aliran'. Apply the same choice in the option C feedback.
questions.3.options.2.text.back: How a river shifted place over a long period
questions.3.options.2.text.source: How a river moved over a long time

questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A river shifting place over hundreds of years is a pattern. A wide view is best for showing it. Look at Lesson 3 again.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A river that moves over hundreds of years is a pattern. A wide view shows this best. Look back at Lesson 3.

questions.4.question.note: Translator: "Account" (origin account, faith account) is "kisah" ("kisah asal usul", "kisah kepercayaan"). Check that it matches Lesson 4, and check the faith wording with care. Back-translation check: 'Account' is 'kisah' (kisah asal usul, kisah kepercayaan). Check that this matches Lesson 4. Because the lesson names faiths, ideally someone from those faiths should check the wording.
questions.4.question.back: Each type of story answers its own type of question. Of the following, which question would a historian ask about an origin story?
questions.4.question.source: Each kind of account answers its own kind of question. Which of these would a historian ask about an origin account?

questions.4.options.0.text.back: How did the sun and planets form?
questions.4.options.0.text.source: How did the sun and the planets form?

questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Scientists ask questions like this about the natural world. Historians ask who told a story, when and why. Look at Lesson 4 again.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Scientists ask questions like this about nature. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Look back at Lesson 4.

questions.4.options.1.feedback.note: Back-translation check: 'Kisah kepercayaan' for 'faith accounts' must match Lesson 4. This is faith-sensitive wording, so it needs a careful native check.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Belief stories and cultural stories often answer questions like this. Historians ask who told a story, and why. Look at Lesson 4 again.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer questions like this. Historians ask who told an account, and why. Look back at Lesson 4.

questions.4.options.2.text.back: Who told this story, and why?
questions.4.options.2.text.source: Who told this account, and why?

questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Historians ask who told a story, when and why. Each type of question needs its own type of answer.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Historians ask who told an account, when and why. Each kind of question needs its own kind of answer.

questions.5.question.note: Translator: The English says "a young person ... she". Malay "dia" has no gender, so "seorang gadis" (a girl) keeps the "she". Check that this is natural. Back-translation check: 'Seorang gadis' keeps the English 'she', but 'gadis' can suggest a young unmarried woman rather than a youth. 'Seorang remaja perempuan' may be better. 'Apakah nama perkara ini?' is literal. Check that it sounds natural.
questions.5.question.back: A girl learns a skill from an older person. She improves the skill. Then she teaches it to her friends. What is this thing called?
questions.5.question.source: A young person learns a skill from an older person. She makes it better. Then she teaches it to her friends. What is this called?

questions.5.options.0.text.note: Translator: "Collective learning" is "pembelajaran kolektif". Check that it matches Lesson 5. "Pembelajaran bersama" is a simpler option. Back-translation check: 'Pembelajaran kolektif' must match Lesson 5. 'Pembelajaran bersama' is simpler for young readers.

questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. In collective learning, people share what they know, improve it and pass it on to other people. This is how knowledge grows.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. In collective learning, people share what they know, make it better and pass it on. This is how knowledge grows.

questions.5.options.1.feedback.note: Back-translation check: This question mixes the standard 'memperbaik/diperbaik' with the everyday 'memperbaikinya' (in the option A and C feedback). Choose one form and use it everywhere.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Trading means you give something and get something in return. Here, a skill is shared and improved. Look at Lesson 5 again.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Trade means you give something and get something back. Here, a skill is shared and made better. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.5.options.2.text.note: Translator: "Foraging" is "mengumpul makanan", as in the Malaysian textbook phrase "memburu dan mengumpul makanan". Check that it matches Lesson 5. The same term is used in Question 8. Back-translation check: 'Foraging' is 'mengumpul makanan'. Check that this matches Lesson 5 and Question 8.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Gathering food means looking for wild food. This example is about sharing a skill and improving it. Look at Lesson 5 again.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Foraging means finding wild food. This example is about sharing a skill and making it better. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.6.question.back: Archaeologists found these clues at an early human site. Which clue can show what people cooked?
questions.6.question.source: Archaeologists found these clues at early human sites. Which clue could show what people cooked?

questions.6.options.0.text.source: The handprints on a rock wall

questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Handprints are a kind of art. They tell us other things, not what people cooked. Look at Lesson 5 again.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Handprints are a kind of art. They tell us other things, not what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.6.options.1.text.note: Translator: "Hearth" is "tungku (api)". Check that young readers know it and that it matches Lesson 5. Back-translation check: 'Tungku (api)' for 'hearth' may make children picture a stove or a cooking stand. Check that it matches Lesson 5 and that young readers will understand it.
questions.6.options.1.text.source: The hearth with its burned seeds

questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. A hearth is a place where people lit fires. Burnt seeds inside the hearth can show what people cooked.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A hearth is a place where people made a fire. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked.

questions.6.options.2.text.back: Tools of the same shape, in places far apart
questions.6.options.2.text.source: Tools of the same shape, far apart

questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. These tools may show that people shared ideas. They do not show what people cooked. Look at Lesson 5 again.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. These tools may show that people shared ideas. They do not show what people cooked. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.7.question.back: After a good harvest, a farming village may have a surplus. What does surplus mean?
questions.7.question.source: After a good harvest, a farming village may have a surplus. What is a surplus?

questions.7.options.0.text.note: Back-translation check: Changed 'pada masa ini' (which could read as 'nowadays') to 'buat masa ini' ('for now'). Check that this keeps the meaning 'right now' in the lesson's past setting. The same change is in the option C feedback.
questions.7.options.0.text.back: Food that is more than what people need at this time
questions.7.options.0.text.source: More food than people need right now

questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. A surplus is extra food. People can store it, so not everyone needs to farm.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A surplus is extra food. People can store it, so not everyone has to farm.

questions.7.options.1.text.back: Plants that people grow to be made into food
questions.7.options.1.text.source: A plant that people grow for food

questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Plants grown to be made into food are crops. A surplus is extra food or goods. Look at Lesson 6 again.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A plant that people grow for food is a crop. A surplus is extra food or goods. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.7.options.2.text.back: Looking for wild food instead of growing it
questions.7.options.2.text.source: Finding wild food instead of growing it

questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Looking for wild food is called gathering food. A surplus is food that is more than what people need at this time. Look at Lesson 6 again.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Finding wild food is called foraging. A surplus is more food than people need right now. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.8.question.back: Banwa is an invented town. Many things changed there over time. Among these changes, which one shows that some people got more power than others?
questions.8.question.source: Banwa is a made-up city. Many things change there over time. Which of these changes shows that some people gained more power than others?

questions.8.options.0.text.back: The farms produced extra grain for several good years
questions.8.options.0.text.source: Farms grow extra grain for several good years

questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Extra grain helped Banwa grow. It does not show who had more power. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Extra grain helped Banwa grow. It does not show who has more power. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.8.options.1.text.back: The residents built a shared storehouse

questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A shared storehouse shows people working together. It does not show who had more power. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A shared storehouse shows people working together. It does not show who has more power. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.8.options.2.text.back: Some families controlled more land and grain
questions.8.options.2.text.source: Some families control more land and grain

questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. Families that had more land and grain had more power. In early towns, power was not shared equally.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Families with more land and grain have more power. In early cities, power was not shared equally.

questions.9.question.note: Translator: "Babylon" is kept as it is in Malaysian Sejarah textbooks. Check against the spelling used in Lesson 7. Back-translation check: Check that 'Babylon' is spelled the same way as in Lesson 7.
questions.9.question.back: In Babylon, King Hammurabi ordered rules to be carved on a tall stone. Everyone had to obey them. What are rules like this called?
questions.9.question.source: In Babylon, King Hammurabi had rules carved on a tall stone. Everyone had to follow them. What are rules like these called?

questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. A tax is something that people give to their government, such as grain or labour. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A tax is something people give to their government, like grain or work. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Correct. Laws are rules that everyone in a particular place must obey. Hammurabi ordered about 280 laws to be carved on a stone.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A law is a rule that everyone in a place must follow. Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a stone.

questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Goods are things that people make or grow, such as jars or cloth. Look at Lesson 7 again.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Goods are things people make or grow, like jars or cloth. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.10.question.note: Translator: "Middle East" is "Timur Tengah". Some Malaysian textbooks say "Asia Barat". Check that it matches Lesson 8. Back-translation check: 'Middle East' is 'Timur Tengah'. Some Malaysian textbooks say 'Asia Barat'. Check that it matches Lesson 8.
questions.10.question.back: Paper was first made in China. How did the idea of making paper reach the Middle East and Europe?
questions.10.question.source: Paper was first made in China. How did the idea of papermaking reach the Middle East and Europe?

questions.10.options.0.text.source: It spread along the trade routes.

questions.10.options.0.feedback.back: Correct. Traders carried ideas as well as goods. The way of making paper spread along those routes to other places.
questions.10.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Papermaking spread along the routes to other lands.

questions.10.options.1.text.back: Every place made it at the same time.
questions.10.options.1.text.source: Each place made it at the same time.

questions.10.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. Paper was first made in China. The idea reached other places later. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.10.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Paper was first made in China. The idea reached other lands later. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.10.options.2.text.back: One trader carried it on one long journey.
questions.10.options.2.text.source: One trader took it on one long trip.

questions.10.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The idea did not arrive in one journey. It moved along trade routes, from one place to one place. Look at Lesson 8 again.
questions.10.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The idea did not travel in one trip. It moved along trade routes, from place to place. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.11.stimulus.title.back: Invented town: a new ticket machine
questions.11.stimulus.title.source: A made-up town: a new ticket machine

questions.11.stimulus.body.back: The invented town of Pellow put a new ticket machine at its bus stop. Before, buying a ticket took 10 minutes. Now, it takes one minute. But its screen displays words in only one language. There are no pictures to help.
questions.11.stimulus.body.source: The made-up town of Pellow puts a new ticket machine at its bus stop. Before, buying a ticket took 10 minutes. Now it takes one minute. But the screen shows words in only one language. It has no pictures to help.

questions.11.question.back: Who might find it hard to use the new machine?
questions.11.question.source: Who might find the new machine hard to use?

questions.11.options.0.text.back: People who want to buy tickets quickly
questions.11.options.0.text.source: People who want to buy tickets quickly

questions.11.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. The machine is faster, so this is a benefit for them. Look at Lesson 9 again.
questions.11.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The machine is faster, so this is a benefit for these people. Look back at Lesson 9.

questions.11.options.1.text.back: People who ride the bus every day
questions.11.options.1.text.source: People who ride the bus every day

questions.11.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite right yet. People who often ride the bus can save time every day. That is a benefit. Look at Lesson 9 again.
questions.11.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. People who ride often can save time every day. That is a benefit. Look back at Lesson 9.

questions.11.options.2.text.back: People who cannot read that language
questions.11.options.2.text.source: People who cannot read that language

questions.11.options.2.feedback.back: Correct. The screen uses only one language, so it becomes a barrier for some people. An invention only helps the people who are able to use it.
questions.11.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The screen uses only one language, so it is a barrier for some people. An invention only helps people who can use it.

results.high.back: Well done. You know a lot about how we learn about the past and how early communities changed.
results.high.source: Well done. You know a lot about how we learn about the past and how early communities changed.

results.middle.back: Good. You answered many questions correctly. Look at the lessons again for the questions that were not quite right yet, and try again if you want.
results.middle.source: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.

results.low.back: Thank you for trying. Look at Lessons 1–9 again, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
results.low.source: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 1–9, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
